---
title: "Why and when to use a randomised controlled trial"
description-meta: "Learn what impact evaluation is, why a randomised controlled trial usually gives the most credible answer, and when to plan one or use another method."
---

::: {.team-note}
## Summary {.unlisted}
This page explains in more detail why experimentation is worth doing and when to plan it. It explains what impact evaluation is and why experimentation - running a randomised controlled trial (RCT) - is usually the preferred way to do it, and when to use one: which questions it can answer, why it has to be planned early, and when it is not the right tool.
:::


::: {.example .romania}
[The running example: North-East Romania]{.tag}

Throughout this site, we come back to one programme developed as part of the [EuroCOMP
Lab](eurocomp.qmd) to show these ideas in practice: a digitalisation grant scheme for
micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) in North-East Romania, run by the Regional
Development Agency with World Bank support.

```{=html}
<div class="facts">
  <div><div class="k">The programme</div><div class="v">EU-funded grants of EUR 15,000&ndash;100,000 for digital tools, equipment, and services</div></div>
  <div><div class="k">Where</div><div class="v">North-East Romania; run by the regional development agency with World Bank support</div></div>
  <div><div class="k">Who is randomised</div><div class="v">Firms: 1,038 eligible MSMEs, pre-screened via an online application survey</div></div>
  <div><div class="k">The design</div><div class="v">Lottery into a treatment group (grants) and a comparison group (no grants): 519 vs. 519, drawn before a notary</div></div>
  <div><div class="k">Outcomes tracked</div><div class="v">Digital adoption (DESI score), revenues, profits, employment, productivity</div></div>
  <div><div class="k">Starting point</div><div class="v">Average DESI score of 4.3 out of 12; 67% of firms name lack of finance as their main obstacle</div></div>
</div>
```

## Monitoring and evaluation (M&E) vs impact evaluation {#monitoring}

::: {.compare}
::: {.col-e}
::: {.col-head}
M&E
:::
::: {.body}
Collect data on inputs, outputs, outcomes and participants to

- Improve day-to-day management and decisions
- Make descriptive before and after comparisons
:::
::: {.verdict}
Describes what is happening, but not whether it is because of the intervention.
:::
:::
::: {.col-e}
::: {.col-head}
Impact evaluation
:::
::: {.body}
Collect data on participants and comparison groups to

- Find the causal impact of a programme
- Find the most effective way to deliver a programme
- Support cost-benefit analysis
:::
::: {.verdict}
Determines impact in a way that can only be attributed to the programme, by
establishing what would have happened without it.
:::
:::
:::

Monitoring and impact evaluation are complements, not alternatives. An impact evaluation should not go ahead without solid monitoring data: who applied, who was selected, who was contracted, and what they invested in. Without that, you cannot tell whether a programme had no effect or was simply never implemented as planned.

## What exactly is the impact of a programme? {#counterfactual}

**Definition.** Impact is what happens after a programme is introduced, minus what would
have happened in its absence, the counterfactual.

**The dilemma.** The counterfactual is a "what if" and is unknown to us. Ideally, we would observe the same applicant twice, once with the programme and once without
it, and compare. That is impossible: each applicant either takes part or does not. Every
impact evaluation method is a way of approximating that missing second observation.

**The solution.** Find a way to construct the counterfactual so impact can be measured.
This can be done in different ways. The page shows different methods of constructing the counterfactual and explains why RCTs are considered the gold standard. 

```{=html}
<figure class="fig-e">
<svg viewBox="0 0 660 300" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" role="img" aria-label="Line chart showing actual outcomes rising faster than the counterfactual after an intervention, with the gap labelled impact">

  <line x1="80" y1="30" x2="80" y2="250" stroke="var(--dg-line)" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <text x="350" y="278" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="12">Time</text>
  <text x="62" y="140" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="12" transform="rotate(-90 62 140)">Outcome</text>

  <line x1="300" y1="30" x2="300" y2="250" stroke="var(--dg-ink-soft)" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/>

  <polyline points="100,220 150,205 200,190 250,175 300,160" fill="none" stroke="var(--dg-ink)" stroke-width="2.5"/>
  <polyline points="300,160 370,133 440,106 510,79 580,52" fill="none" stroke="var(--dg-accent)" stroke-width="3.5"/>
  <polyline points="300,160 370,150 440,140 510,130 580,120" fill="none" stroke="var(--dg-ink)" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-dasharray="6 5"/>

  <path d="M598 52 H606 M598 120 H606 M602 52 V120" stroke="var(--dg-ink)" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"/>
  <text x="614" y="90" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="13" font-weight="bold">Impact</text>

  <text x="500" y="40" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="12" font-weight="bold">Actual</text>
```

### Impact is measured using outcomes

When evaluating projects, often only outputs are assessed, because they are the easiest
thing to count. Measuring impact means moving from counting outputs to measuring outcomes.

::: {.cards}
::: {.card-e}
#### Outputs
What a programme delivers.
For example, grants disbursed, firms enrolled, training sessions run.
:::
::: {.card-e}
#### Outcomes
What changes because of it.
For example, growth, jobs, innovation, resilience.
:::
:::



::: {.example .romania}
[The impact in the North-East Romania programme]{.tag}

For North-East Romania, the impact is the gap between treatment and comparison firms on
four tracked outcomes: digital adoption, revenue, employment, and productivity.

Before implementation, map out how a programme's activities are expected to change the problem you are addressing. That shows, in advance, why each step should lead to the next. That causal logic, the how and why behind each step, explains a programme's reason for existing. It also tells you what you need to measure in order to test whether the
expected change is actually happening.

```{=html}
<div class="chain">
  <div class="step"><b>Inputs</b></div>
  <span class="flow-arrow" aria-hidden="true">&rarr;</span>
  <div class="step"><b>Activities</b></div>
  <span class="flow-arrow" aria-hidden="true">&rarr;</span>
  <div class="step"><b>Outputs</b></div>
  <span class="flow-arrow" aria-hidden="true">&rarr;</span>
  <div class="on"><b>Outcomes</b></div>
</div>
```

But which outcomes should one look at exactly? A programme can change many things, and not all of them can or should be measured. To know which outcomes to look at, and when to expect them to change, start by spelling out how the programme is supposed to work: how its inputs and activities lead to outputs, and how those outputs are expected to lead to outcomes. Doing this before implementation shows, in advance, why each step should lead to the next, and tells you what to measure to test whether the expected change is actually happening.

This chain is the foundation of a theory of change, and having thought it through helps
in designing a strong impact evaluation. There is more on this in
[Step 1: develop a Theory of Change](02.01-toc.qmd). 

Making the chain explicit also surfaces the assumptions behind each link, and shows which of them the programme's impact depends on most. If one of these assumptions does not hold (for example, that firms will take up the support they are offered), the programme may fall short of its intended impact. One way to reduce this risk is to test, within the same evaluation, alternative ways of addressing that weak link, such as two different outreach approaches, and see which works better.

::: {.example .case #digitrans}
[Digitrans example]{.tag}
The Digitrans pilot (see [Examples](03-examples.qmd) for more details) tested and compared two alternative ways to increase digital adoption among MSMEs in Bulgaria, Poland and Slovakia. Firms were randomly assigned to either (i) a comparison group receiving no support, (ii) a financial subsidy alone, or (iii) the same subsidy paired with technical assistance.

The pilot found that money alone was not the most effective approach. Firms that also received technical assistance used
digital tools 2.5 times more intensively than those with the subsidy alone. This is evidence that capability, not just cash, was a constraint to digitalisation. 
:::

## What does good allocation of public resources look like? {#allocation}

Return on public investment is the benefit attributable to a programme divided by its
cost. "Attributable" requires knowing what the programme beneficiaries would have done in the absence of the programme (the counterfactual).

That is especially hard when beneficiaries are not assigned to programmes at random but are selected by the Managing Authority. Beneficiaries may differ from those that were not selected, e.g. they may be more motivated or have more resources. Most of these traits
are never recorded in any database or questionnaire. When the beneficiaries later do better on the outcomes of interest than the applicants that were not selected,
it is impossible to tell how much of that difference is due to the programme.

Consider an illustrative innovation-grant scheme: EUR 50,000 to each of 100 firms, where
"success" means launching a new product. Compare two selection rules.

::: {.compare}
::: {.col-e}
::: {.col-head}
Strategy A: fund the top performers
:::
::: {.body}
Firms that succeed: **80 of 100**

Would have succeeded anyway: **65**

Succeeded because of the grant: **15**

Additionality rate: **19%**
:::
::: {.verdict}
Strategy A looks stronger at the first glance as it is associated with 80 successes but only 15 of these succeeded because of the grant.
:::
:::
::: {.col-e}
::: {.col-head}
Strategy B: fund the marginal firm
:::
::: {.body}
Firms that succeed: **55 of 100**

Would have succeeded anyway: **20**

Succeeded because of the grant: **35**

Additionality rate: **64%**
:::
::: {.verdict}
Strategy B causes 35 successes and thus is more impactful than A. 
:::
:::
:::

Raw success counts can be misleading. Programmes need to be judged on impact, not on raw success to evaluate their effectiveness.

::: {.cards}
::: {.card-e}
### Deadweight: low additionality {.unlisted}
Additionality is the share of activity that would not have happened without the programme. Top performers would likely have invested anyway, so public funds mostly substitute for money they would have spent regardless - generating little that is truly additional per euro.
:::
::: {.card-e}
### Selection bias in measurement {.unlisted}
Comparing funded, stronger firms with unfunded, weaker ones credits the programme with
firms' pre-existing quality, not with what the grant did.
:::
::: {.card-e}
### Where the grant buys most {.unlisted}
Support actually changes behaviour for the marginal, constrained firm: the good project
that could not otherwise get funded.
:::
::: {.card-e}
### Can experts spot the marginal firm? {.unlisted}
Evidence suggests not reliably. In a business plan competition in Nigeria, judges' scores
did not predict which firms would survive or grow three years later (McKenzie & Sansone,
2019; see [Common myths](index.qmd#common-myths-about-rcts)).
:::
:::

## Finding the counterfactual  {#finding-counterfactual}

As [defined above](#counterfactual), the counterfactual is what would have happened to programme participants without the programme. It can never be observed directly, so it has to be estimated.

**Strategy.** Find a group of firms that on average look like treated firms would have
looked in the absence of the programme. This group is the comparison group.

There are two ways of estimating the counterfactual:

::: {.compare}
::: {.col-e}
::: {.col-head}
Ex-ante: Randomised controlled trials
:::
::: {.body}
Create the comparison group up front, by randomly assigning who receives the programme.
Randomisation is what guarantees the two groups look the same on average.
:::
:::
::: {.col-e}
::: {.col-head}
Ex-post: quasi-experimental designs
:::
::: {.body}
Look for a suitable comparison group after the programme has already been rolled out,
using natural variation in who received the programme and who did not.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.caution}
**Selection bias** is the risk that the comparison group does not actually look like the
treatment group on average. If that assumption is wrong, the impact estimate is biased.
:::

::: {.example .romania}
[North-East Romania: the counterfactual]{.tag}
In North-East Romania, the counterfactual is the group of eligible firms that were not
drawn in the lottery. [How the lottery created it](#rct).
:::

## What is a randomised controlled trial? {#rct}

**Intuition.** Randomly assign the programme so one group receives it (the treatment
group) and one does not (the comparison group). Because the two groups start
out the same, the comparison group's outcome shows what would have happened to the treatment
group without the programme.

```{=html}
<figure class="fig-e">
<svg viewBox="0 0 660 300" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" role="img" aria-label="Treatment and comparison groups start at the same outcome level and diverge after the programme, with the gap labelled impact">
  <line x1="80" y1="250" x2="620" y2="250" stroke="var(--dg-line)" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <line x1="80" y1="30" x2="80" y2="250" stroke="var(--dg-line)" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <text x="350" y="278" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="12">Time</text>
  <text x="62" y="140" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="12" transform="rotate(-90 62 140)">Outcome</text>

  <line x1="300" y1="30" x2="300" y2="250" stroke="var(--dg-ink-soft)" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/>
  <text x="300" y="22" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="12" font-weight="bold">Programme starts</text>
  <text x="190" y="270" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="11.5">Pre</text>
  <text x="450" y="270" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="11.5">Post</text>

  <polyline points="110,200 200,195 300,190" fill="none" stroke="var(--dg-ink)" stroke-width="2.5"/>
  <polyline points="300,190 390,155 480,120 570,85" fill="none" stroke="var(--dg-accent)" stroke-width="3.5"/>
  <polyline points="300,190 390,182 480,174 570,166" fill="none" stroke="var(--dg-ink)" stroke-width="2.5"/>

  <circle cx="110" cy="200" r="5" fill="var(--dg-ink)"/>
  <text x="122" y="192" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="11.5">Same starting point</text>

  <path d="M588 85 H596 M588 166 H596 M592 85 V166" stroke="var(--dg-ink)" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"/>
  <text x="604" y="129" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="13" font-weight="bold">Impact</text>

  <text x="480" y="72" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="12" font-weight="bold">Treatment group</text>
  <text x="480" y="200" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="12">Comparison group</text>
</svg>
<figcaption>Note: Treatment and comparison groups start at the same outcome level and diverge after the programme, with the divergence being the impact of a programme.</figcaption>
</figure>
```
Because assignment is decided by chance, the two groups are alike on average not only in characteristics you can measure, but also in those you cannot. Take the example of firms applying for a grant: randomising who receives the money means that, on average, the two groups look the same on observable characteristics such as size, sector or turnover, and also on unobservable ones such as management quality or motivation. Nothing should systematically differ between them except that some applicants were lucky in the draw and others were not. That is why no statistical adjustment for firm characteristics is needed to get a credible estimate.

::: {.soft-panel}
**What "random" means here.** Not randomly sampling a sub-population to study, but
randomly deciding, among qualifying applicants, who receives the programme and who
does not.
:::

**Advantage.** RCTs are considered the gold standard of quantitative impact evaluation
because:

- No assumptions about outcome levels or trends between groups are necessary, as long as randomisation is implemented correctly
- They deliver strong evidence
- They are easy to interpret


::: {.example .romania}
[North-East Romania: the lottery and its comparison group]{.tag}

Firms first completed an online pre-assessment survey. The 1,038 firms that met the
pre-set eligibility criteria all qualified. Because demand exceeded the budget, a public
lottery decided which 519 would be invited to apply formally; the other 519 formed the
comparison group.

Before any grants were awarded, the two groups were statistically identical:

| | Not selected | Selected |
|---|---|---|
| Average DESI score (0-12) | 4.30 | 4.30 |
| Average employees, 2022 (admin data) | 13.8 | 13.8 |
| Share with fewer than 10 employees | 63% | 63% |
| Share in urban areas | 84% | 84% |


Because the groups started out the same, the difference between them over time is the
impact of being invited to apply for the grant.

## Randomisation can improve legitimacy and trust in programmes {#legitimacy}

Randomly selecting beneficiaries among eligible applicants is fair. When more applications are eligible than there is budget to fund, a lottery is a transparent way to decide who gets in. It treats every eligible applicant the same rather than relying on favouritism or timing.

Illustration:
```{=html}
<div class="funnel">
  <figure>
    <figcaption>Firms that apply</figcaption>
    <div class="n">24 firms apply</div>
    <div class="dots"><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span></div>
  </figure>
  <figure>
    <figcaption>Firms that are eligible</figcaption>
    <div class="n">10 meet the threshold</div>
    <div class="dots"><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span></span><span></span><span></span><span></span><span></span><span></span><span></span><span></span><span></span><span></span><span></span><span></span><span></span><span></span></div>
  </figure>
  <figure>
    <figcaption>Firms selected</figcaption>
    <div class="n">4 are randomly selected</div>
    <div class="dots"><span class="b"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="b"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="b"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="b"></span><span class="a"></span><span></span><span></span><span></span><span></span><span></span><span></span><span></span><span></span><span></span><span></span><span></span><span></span><span></span><span></span></div>
  </figure>
</div>
```

::: {.example .romania}
[North-East Romania: additional measures to increase trust]{.tag}

North-East Romania's draw was run in front of a notary: the random number seed drawn, the
selection code run, and the resulting balance between groups reviewed. This increased firms' confidence that selection was fair.
The draw also made selection faster. Because beneficiaries were drawn at random from the
eligible pool, no ranking of the "best" applications was needed. Evaluators only had to
check that each firm met the formal criteria and that the requested funds were justified.
:::

## What do you want to learn? {#two-questions}

Whether you have sufficient evidence that your programme works, or you are still working
out who it reaches and how to design it, there is a case for experimentation. The starting
question is whether the programme is working as well as it could be.

::: {.compare}
::: {.col-e}
::: {.col-head}
Does the programme cause an effect at all?
:::
::: {.body}
You do not yet know whether the programme works, or you are still working out
who it reaches and how it should be designed before it starts. This requires finding a
credible comparison group before the programme launches. Example: in North-East Romania,
a lottery decided which eligible firms were invited to apply for a digitalisation grant,
and the others formed the comparison group ([see above](#rct)).
:::
:::
::: {.col-e}
::: {.col-head}
How do you deliver it better?
:::
::: {.body}
You already know the programme works. The programme's implementation may already be ongoing. What you want to know is which version of the programme works
best. Example: The [Digitrans example](#digitrans) compares whether a grant alone versus a grant combined with
technical assistance performs best.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.example .romania}
[North-East Romania: testing outreach]{.tag}
In fact, the North-East Romania programme asked both questions. It used an experiment to find out if the programme is effective and a second experiment to study how to best conduct outreach.
Before the digitalisation call, the regional development agency randomly selected 26 of 46
towns for in-person information visits, in which a consultant explained the call and
helped firms complete the pre-assessment survey. The visited towns produced 110
applications against 71 in the towns that did not receive in-person visits (55% more). The additional applicants in towns with in-person visits were
smaller firms (12.6 employees on average, compared with 19.6).
:::

::: {.example .case}
[Colombia: group vs individual management support]{.tag}
[Iacovone et al. 2022](03-examples.qmd#colombia-scaling-up-management-consulting) compared two ways to deliver management consulting to auto-parts firms:
one-to-one (about US$28,950 per firm) and in groups of 3-8 firms (about US$10,500). Both
raised management scores by around 9 percentage points, but only group consulting
significantly raised sales and profits.

:::

## What if you cannot randomise? {#alternatives}

For the question of whether a programme has an effect at all, an RCT only works if randomisation is built in from day one, integrated at design stage before the programme launches (ex-ante), not added afterwards. The comparison group, sample size, and data to collect all depend on those early decisions. When early randomisation for this question is not possible,
quasi-experimental methods are the alternative as these are usually conducted after a programme (ex-post). This section provides an overview of the most common quasi-experimental methods. 

However, if what you want to know is how best to run a programme that is already launched, rather than whether it works at all, this constraint does not bind in the same way ([see above](#two-questions)). 

::: {.caution}
Quasi-experimental methods always rely on assumptions, some stronger than others. If those
assumptions do not hold, the impact estimate is biased. Many of these assumptions are not
testable. The credibility of the evaluation depends on the credibility of the assumptions made.
:::

::::: {.myths-grid .methods}

<details class="myth-box" id="pre-post-before-and-after">
<summary>Pre-post (before and after)</summary>

::: {.method}
Method
: Compare programme participants before and after the programme.

Identifying assumption
: In the absence of the programme, participants would have had the same measured outcomes
as before. That means no other factors or events, for example economic shocks, affect the
outcome besides the programme. This is a strong assumption that rarely holds in practice.

::: {.eg}
For example, sales might rise after a grant simply because the whole regional economy is
recovering at the same time, not because of the programme.
:::
:::

```{=html}
<figure class="fig-e">
<svg viewBox="0 0 660 260" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" role="img" aria-label="Pre-post design assumes a flat comparison line, so the whole rise is attributed to the programme">
  <line x1="80" y1="215" x2="620" y2="215" stroke="var(--dg-line)" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <line x1="80" y1="25" x2="80" y2="215" stroke="var(--dg-line)" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <text x="350" y="243" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="12">Time</text>
  <line x1="280" y1="25" x2="280" y2="215" stroke="var(--dg-ink-soft)" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/>
  <text x="280" y="18" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="12" font-weight="bold">Intervention</text>

  <polyline points="110,180 280,170" fill="none" stroke="var(--dg-ink)" stroke-width="2.5"/>
  <polyline points="280,170 380,140 480,110 570,80" fill="none" stroke="var(--dg-accent)" stroke-width="3.5"/>
  <polyline points="280,170 570,170" fill="none" stroke="var(--dg-ink-soft)" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="6 5"/>
  <text x="400" y="188" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="11.5">Comparison assumed flat</text>

  <path d="M588 80 H596 M588 170 H596 M592 80 V170" stroke="var(--dg-ink)" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"/>
  <text x="604" y="120" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="12" font-weight="bold">Pre-post</text>
  <text x="604" y="136" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="12" font-weight="bold">impact</text>
</svg>
<figcaption>Note: A before-and-after comparison assumes that, without the programme, outcomes would have stayed flat. Any change in the meantime is counted as impact.</figcaption>
</figure>
```

</details>

<details class="myth-box" id="simple-difference">
<summary>Simple difference</summary>

::: {.method}
Method
: Compare programme participants with non-participants.

Identifying assumption
: There is no difference between participants and non-participants besides programme
participation. The reason for participation must be unrelated to outcomes. Again, this is
unlikely to hold in practice.

::: {.eg}
For example, firms that apply for a grant are often more ambitious or better managed than
those that do not, so they might grow faster regardless of the grant.
:::
:::

```{=html}
<figure class="fig-e">
<svg viewBox="0 0 660 250" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" role="img" aria-label="Participants show higher outcomes than non-participants. The gap, the simple difference, mixes the programme effect with an unobserved difference that was there all along, for example firm quality">
  <line x1="90" y1="205" x2="600" y2="205" stroke="var(--dg-line)" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <line x1="90" y1="25" x2="90" y2="205" stroke="var(--dg-line)" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <text x="72" y="115" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="12" transform="rotate(-90 72 115)">Outcome</text>

  <rect x="180" y="130" width="110" height="75" fill="var(--dg-accent-dark)"/>
  <rect x="180" y="95" width="110" height="35" fill="var(--dg-accent)" fill-opacity="0.4"/>
  <rect x="180" y="60" width="110" height="35" fill="var(--dg-accent)"/>
  <text x="235" y="225" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="12.5" font-weight="bold">Participants</text>

  <rect x="440" y="130" width="110" height="75" fill="var(--dg-ink)"/>
  <text x="495" y="225" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="12.5" font-weight="bold">Non-participants</text>

  <line x1="290" y1="60" x2="568" y2="60" stroke="var(--dg-ink-soft)" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/>
  <line x1="290" y1="130" x2="440" y2="130" stroke="var(--dg-ink-soft)" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/>

  <text x="300" y="82" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="11.5" font-weight="bold">Programme effect</text>
  <text x="300" y="109" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="11.5">Unobserved difference,</text>
  <text x="300" y="123" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="11.5">for example firm quality</text>

  <path d="M572 60 H580 M572 130 H580 M576 60 V130" stroke="var(--dg-ink)" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"/>
  <text x="588" y="90" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="12" font-weight="bold">Simple</text>
  <text x="588" y="106" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="12" font-weight="bold">difference</text>
</svg>
<figcaption>Note: The measured gap mixes the programme effect with differences that were there all along.</figcaption>
</figure>
```

</details>

<details class="myth-box" id="difference-in-differences">
<summary>Difference in differences</summary>

::: {.method}
Method
: Find a group with the same trend and compare differences over time.

Identifying assumption
: Any other factors affecting participants over time are the same for non-participants, so
both groups would follow the same trajectory in the absence of treatment. This is the
parallel trends assumption, and it cannot be tested.

::: {.eg}
For example, if grant recipients are concentrated in areas hit harder by a regional
downturn than the comparison firms, their trends could diverge even without the programme.
:::
:::

```{=html}
<figure class="fig-e">
<svg viewBox="0 0 660 260" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" role="img" aria-label="Treatment and comparison groups both rise, but the treatment group rises further; the difference between the two changes is the estimate">
  <line x1="80" y1="215" x2="620" y2="215" stroke="var(--dg-line)" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <line x1="80" y1="25" x2="80" y2="215" stroke="var(--dg-line)" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <text x="350" y="243" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="12">Time</text>
  <line x1="290" y1="25" x2="290" y2="215" stroke="var(--dg-ink-soft)" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/>
  <text x="290" y="18" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="12" font-weight="bold">Intervention</text>

  <polyline points="120,150 290,130" fill="none" stroke="var(--dg-accent)" stroke-width="3.5"/>
  <polyline points="290,130 560,60" fill="none" stroke="var(--dg-accent)" stroke-width="3.5"/>
  <polyline points="120,190 290,175" fill="none" stroke="var(--dg-ink)" stroke-width="2.5"/>
  <polyline points="290,175 560,145" fill="none" stroke="var(--dg-ink)" stroke-width="2.5"/>

  <path d="M578 60 H586 M578 130 H586 M582 60 V130" stroke="var(--dg-ink)" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"/>
  <text x="594" y="99" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="11.5" font-weight="bold">Diff 1</text>
  <path d="M578 145 H586 M578 175 H586 M582 145 V175" stroke="var(--dg-ink-soft)" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"/>
  <text x="594" y="164" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="11.5">Diff 2</text>

  <text x="380" y="52" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="12" font-weight="bold">Treatment group</text>
  <text x="380" y="178" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="12">Comparison group</text>
</svg>
<figcaption>Note: The estimate is Difference 1 minus Difference 2: how much more the treatment group changed than the comparison group.</figcaption>
</figure>
```

</details>

<details class="myth-box" id="matching">
<summary>Matching</summary>

::: {.method}
Method
: Participants are matched with non-participants who share the same observable
characteristics. Matching tries to mimic an RCT. It can be done in different ways: a
participant can be matched with one non-participant, or with a weighted average of all
similar non-participants, where closer matches count more.

Identifying assumption
: There are no differences between participants and matched non-participants in
unobserved characteristics that affect the outcome.

::: {.eg}
For example, two firms matched on size and sector might still differ in the owner's
ambition or management quality, both of which would likely affect outcomes.
:::
:::

</details>

<details class="myth-box" id="regression-discontinuity-design">
<summary>Regression discontinuity design</summary>

::: {.method}
Method
: Compare participants who were just eligible with those who were just ineligible. This
does not measure impact for all participants, only for those at the cut-off, which is why
the result is called a local average treatment effect. The advantage is that unobservable
characteristics stop being a concern.

Identifying assumption
: This design assumes that

    - the programme is administered following pre-defined cut-off rules
    - the criteria determining who falls above or below are not manipulated
    - a large number of units sit around the cut-off
    - nothing else changes suddenly at the cut-off

::: {.eg}
For example, if firms know grants are awarded below a certain revenue threshold, some
might understate revenue slightly to stay just below it, so firms just below the cut-off
are no longer comparable to those just above.
:::
:::

```{=html}
<figure class="fig-e">
<svg viewBox="0 0 660 260" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" role="img" aria-label="Outcomes jump discontinuously at the eligibility cutoff">
  <line x1="80" y1="215" x2="620" y2="215" stroke="var(--dg-line)" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <line x1="80" y1="25" x2="80" y2="215" stroke="var(--dg-line)" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <text x="350" y="243" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="12">Cut-off variable</text>
  <text x="62" y="120" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="12" transform="rotate(-90 62 120)">Outcome</text>

  <line x1="350" y1="25" x2="350" y2="215" stroke="var(--dg-ink-soft)" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/>
  <text x="350" y="18" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="12" font-weight="bold">Cut-off</text>

  <circle cx="130" cy="180" r="4" fill="var(--dg-ink)"/><circle cx="165" cy="172" r="4" fill="var(--dg-ink)"/>
  <circle cx="200" cy="178" r="4" fill="var(--dg-ink)"/><circle cx="235" cy="163" r="4" fill="var(--dg-ink)"/>
  <circle cx="270" cy="168" r="4" fill="var(--dg-ink)"/><circle cx="305" cy="156" r="4" fill="var(--dg-ink)"/>
  <circle cx="335" cy="160" r="4" fill="var(--dg-ink)"/>
  <polyline points="120,182 345,158" fill="none" stroke="var(--dg-ink)" stroke-width="2.5"/>

  <circle cx="365" cy="108" r="4" fill="var(--dg-accent)"/><circle cx="400" cy="112" r="4" fill="var(--dg-accent)"/>
  <circle cx="435" cy="98" r="4" fill="var(--dg-accent)"/><circle cx="470" cy="104" r="4" fill="var(--dg-accent)"/>
  <circle cx="505" cy="90" r="4" fill="var(--dg-accent)"/><circle cx="540" cy="95" r="4" fill="var(--dg-accent)"/>
  <circle cx="575" cy="84" r="4" fill="var(--dg-accent)"/>
  <polyline points="355,110 585,86" fill="none" stroke="var(--dg-accent)" stroke-width="3.5"/>

  <path d="M338 110 H346 M338 158 H346 M342 110 V158" stroke="var(--dg-ink)" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"/>
  <text x="250" y="128" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="12" font-weight="bold">RDD effect</text>
</svg>
<figcaption>Note: This method requires many applicants sitting close to the cut-off, so those just below and just above can be meaningfully compared.</figcaption>
</figure>
```

</details>

:::::

## When not to run an RCT {#when-not}

::: {.cards}
::: {.card-e}
[01]{.num}

### Not the right tool {.unlisted}
The question is excellent but is not about impact, for example satisfaction with services
or cost per service. Monitoring and feedback data are easier and do not need a counterfactual.
:::
::: {.card-e}
[02]{.num}

### Not yet {.unlisted}
The theory of change is not clear, or implementation is unlikely to work because the
markets to serve do not exist.
:::
::: {.card-e}
[03]{.num}

### Statistically not feasible {.unlisted}
Too few units or too little money. Large indirect or spillover effects you cannot measure (Spillovers alone are not a
reason to drop an RCT: if expected, they can be designed for and measured (see
[Step 4: check whether an RCT is feasible](02.03-assess.qmd)))
Setting too chaotic, for example disaster relief. Treatment assigned at too high a level,
for example national policy.
:::
::: {.card-e}
[04]{.num}

### Maybe not worth it for learning {.unlisted}
The answer is already known from credible existing studies, or there is no generalisable
"why" because the programme is one-off with little scale or replication potential.
:::
:::

If an RCT is the right tool in principle, [Step 4: check whether an RCT is feasible](02.03-assess.qmd) checks whether it is
feasible in practice: oversubscription, timing, legal basis, institutional buy-in and
measurable outcomes.

## Learning through RCTs is a continuous process {#learning-cycle}

Every RCT raises new questions along with the ones it answers, each round building
on the last. That is how we expand our knowledge of what works, for whom, and under what
conditions, and use it to design better programmes. Exchange within a community of practice
matters, so we can learn from each other, not just from our own results. 

But before adopting what worked elsewhere, questions of external validity need to be considered, as what worked in one place may not necessarily work in another. One needs to ask: are the conditions comparable, i.e. is the target group similar and are the conditions essential to that result actually in place in my setting? 

```{=html}
<figure class="fig-e">
<svg viewBox="0 0 660 300" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" role="img" aria-label="A four stage cycle: review evidence and create learnings, design, test, adjust and invest">
  <defs>
    <marker id="ah" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="8" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto">
      <path d="M0 0 L10 5 L0 10 z" fill="var(--dg-line)"/>
    </marker>
  </defs>
  <path d="M370 60 Q510 90 530 148" stroke="var(--dg-line)" stroke-width="2" fill="none" marker-end="url(#ah)"/>
  <path d="M530 200 Q505 258 380 240" stroke="var(--dg-line)" stroke-width="2" fill="none" marker-end="url(#ah)"/>
  <path d="M270 240 Q150 258 128 200" stroke="var(--dg-line)" stroke-width="2" fill="none" marker-end="url(#ah)"/>
  <path d="M128 148 Q150 90 275 62" stroke="var(--dg-line)" stroke-width="2" fill="none" marker-end="url(#ah)"/>

  <rect x="255" y="30" width="150" height="52" rx="6" fill="var(--dg-accent)"/>
  <text x="330" y="51" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="12.5" font-weight="bold">Review evidence,</text>
  <text x="330" y="68" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="12.5" font-weight="bold">create learnings</text>

  <rect x="470" y="152" width="150" height="42" rx="6" fill="var(--dg-panel)" stroke="var(--dg-rule)"/>
  <text x="545" y="178" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="14" font-weight="bold">Design</text>

  <rect x="255" y="228" width="150" height="42" rx="6" fill="var(--dg-panel)" stroke="var(--dg-rule)"/>
  <text x="330" y="254" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="14" font-weight="bold">Test</text>

  <rect x="40" y="152" width="150" height="42" rx="6" fill="var(--dg-panel)" stroke="var(--dg-rule)"/>
  <text x="115" y="178" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="13.5" font-weight="bold">Adjust and invest</text>
</svg>
<figcaption>Note: Testing new policies and learning from previous programmes are integral for designing effective and efficient policies.</figcaption>
</figure>
```

::: {.cards}
::: {.card-e}
[Review]{.num}
Before considering how to embed an RCT, review a programme's [theory of change](02.01-toc.qmd), identify risks and the [learning questions](02.02-eval_questions.qmd) this round should answer, and the [outcomes](09-bank_outcomes.qmd) most likely to change.
Review lessons from other [settings and countries](03-examples.qmd) and adapt them.
Identify baseline needs of potential beneficiaries in your region.
:::
::: {.card-e}
[Design]{.num}
Choose a credible comparison group and set the [sample size](02.03a-power.qmd) needed to detect a meaningful effect.
Turn the outcomes identified in Review into [measurable indicators](02.04-indicators.qmd) using [primary and secondary data](02.05-data_sources.qmd), and set out the [data collection](02.06-data_collect.qmd) plan, budget, and timeline in a [Terms of Reference](02.06a-tor.qmd).
:::
::: {.card-e}
[Test]{.num}
Test different programme designs and delivery modes to identify what works best.
Assess for whom the programme works best. Address take-up challenges. Learn about mechanisms, unintended effects, and crowding out.
:::
::: {.card-e}
[Invest]{.num}
Get a quantitative and credible impact estimate that can guide future investments.
Conduct cost-benefit analyses to avoid wasting money and to inform programme decisions.
Scale up based on evidence.
:::
:::
